cake-or-cupcake-white-with-chocolate-ici.title: Cake or cupcake, white with chocolate icing

content.title: About
content.content: Cake or cupcake is a soft sponge‑based pastry topped with a white buttercream layer and finished with chocolate icing. It is produced in bakeries and commonly served as a dessert with tea or coffee.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The white buttercream is often made from cream cheese, heavy cream and vanilla, giving it a delicate flavor.
Chocolate icing can be dark or milk chocolate, depending on customer preference.
Cakes and cupcakes are frequently decorated with sprinkles, nuts or berries for flavor and visual contrast.
Some bakeries use natural cocoa butter instead of vegetable fats in the icing.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The buttercream base contains calcium, which supports bone health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The egg‑ and flour‑based batter provides vitamins B2 and B6, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate icing, especially dark chocolate, supplies flavonoids with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cream and icing contain milk, which can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Cakes and cupcakes are often sweet; excessive intake may contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The batter typically uses wheat flour, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake or cupcake as a dessert after a meal, pair it with tea or coffee, or use it as a layer in a celebratory cake assembly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage (up to 5 days) refrigerate. Before eating, check for any signs of mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Cauliflower is a cruciferous vegetable that, after harvesting, is blanched, flash‑frozen and enriched with added fat to improve flavor and texture. The product is ready to eat after heating and retains most of the nutrients found in fresh cauliflower.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cauliflower is rich in B‑vitamins, vitamin C and dietary fiber.
Freezing preserves up to 90 % of vitamin C, which is lost during prolonged storage of fresh heads.
Added fat enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin K.
It is a staple in low‑calorie diets because of its low energy density and high fiber content.
In some regions cauliflower is colloquially called “white cabbage.”

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress and strengthening the immune system.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Fiber promotes regular bowel movements and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Cholesterol reduction
items.content: Phytochemicals in cauliflower help lower LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Weight management
items.content: Low calorie content and high satiety make it suitable for weight‑control diets.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to cauliflower.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The added fat should be considered by those monitoring their fat intake.

items.title: Moisture formation
items.content: Improper storage can lead to ice crystal formation, affecting texture after reheating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the product by steaming, microwaving, or boiling for 5–7 minutes. Serve as a side dish, add to soups, stews, casseroles, or blend into a puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C or lower. Once opened, use within 3–4 months. Do not thaw and refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean, boneless cut taken from the bird's chest. When sautéed with a little oil, the skin stays crisp and adds flavor. The dish is high in protein and relatively low in fat when prepared without excess oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast is the most consumed chicken cut worldwide because of its low calorie density and high protein content.
When cooked with the skin, the crisp layer retains some B‑vitamins that are naturally present in the skin.
The meat is easily digestible and often recommended in muscle‑building diets.
Different cuisines season it variously—from simple salt and pepper to paprika, garlic, and fresh herbs.
In French cuisine, chicken breast is sometimes sautéed in butter with a splash of white wine for a richer flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 31 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When cooked properly, the skin absorbs minimal added fat, making the dish suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken breast contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, immune function, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The high protein content promotes prolonged fullness, helping with weight management.

items.title: Fat over‑consumption
items.content: Using too much oil or cooking on high heat can cause the skin to soak up excess fat, raising the calorie count.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C to eliminate salmonella risk.

items.title: Chicken protein allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt or soy‑based sauces can increase sodium levels, which may be problematic for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauteed chicken breast with skin can be served as a main course, sliced for salads, added to sandwiches, or tossed with pasta. For a lighter option, trim some of the crisp skin after cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked breast to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container. Refrigerate for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for 2‑3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate candy with caramel filling consists of small sweets coated in milk or dark chocolate and filled with a soft caramel center. They are popular as a treat for both children and adults and are often sold in 100‑200 g packages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The caramel filling is usually made from sugar, butter, and cream, giving it a buttery flavor and smooth texture.
Chocolate candies are frequently used as ingredients in desserts such as cakes, ice cream, and cupcakes.
Caramel candies originated in Europe in the 19th century, and chocolate‑coated versions became mass‑produced after the invention of the conching process.
In some countries, caramel‑filled chocolate candies are a traditional gift for holidays like New Year’s.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugar and fats in the candy provide quick energy, which can be useful in situations requiring rapid fuel.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate, especially dark chocolate, contains flavonoids that have antioxidant properties and may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: The sugar and theobromine in chocolate stimulate serotonin production, helping to improve mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to tooth decay, weight gain, and elevated blood glucose levels.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: These candies often contain milk chocolate and butter, which may trigger reactions in people allergic to dairy.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Chocolate candies can be high in saturated fats, which, when consumed excessively, may negatively affect cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Candies can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to baked goods, ice cream, or used as decoration for desserts. Moderate consumption is recommended due to their high sugar and fat content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the candies in a cool, dry place in an airtight container, protected from direct sunlight. At temperatures above 25 °C chocolate may melt and the caramel can become sticky.

content.title: About
content.content: Chow mein and Chop suey are popular Asian‑style dishes consisting of stir‑fried noodles and vegetables with a variety of meats (chicken, beef, pork, shrimp). Thin egg or wheat noodles are quickly cooked over high heat to stay slightly crisp. The dishes are usually finished with soy sauce, ginger and garlic, giving them a distinctive aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chow mein originated in China in the early 1900s and became widespread in the United States thanks to Chinese immigrants.
In the U.S. Chop suey is often thought of as “Chinese stew,” while in China the dish is known as “chow cai” and varies regionally.
Traditional chow mein noodles are hand‑pulled, but mass‑produced versions use dried noodles that are pre‑boiled before stir‑frying.
Seafood versions (shrimp, calamari) are considered more “premium” and are common in upscale restaurants.
Japan’s counterpart to chow mein is “yakisoba,” a stir‑fried noodle dish with soy sauce and vegetables.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Meat and seafood provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken, beef and soy sauce contain vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat and spinach, often added to chop suey, are good sources of iron needed for blood formation.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The dish is prepared without sugar, making it suitable for moderate carbohydrate intake.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Vegetables such as carrots, bell pepper and broccoli increase dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and ready‑made seasoning mixes can be high in salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp and other seafood commonly used may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some pre‑made sauces contain added MSG, which can cause headaches in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Processed noodles
items.content: Dried noodles may contain preservatives; for a cleaner option choose fresh noodles or make them at home.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, straight from the wok. It can be enjoyed on its own or alongside steamed rice. Garnish with fresh lime, sliced green onions or toasted sesame seeds to boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Leftover chow mein or chop suey should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator and eaten within 2–3 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a splash of water to restore noodle moisture.

corn-canned-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Corn, canned, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Canned cooked corn with no added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product made from mature corn kernels that are boiled, cooled and sealed in airtight cans. No oils or fats are added during processing, so the corn retains its natural flavor and nutritional profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the world’s most widely consumed vegetables, and it has been canned for over a century.
Cooked canned corn retains about 90 % of its vitamin C, which is lost quickly in fresh corn during storage.
Cans usually contain only a small amount of salt for taste, and the amount is regulated by food standards.
The bright yellow color comes from carotenoid antioxidants.
Canned corn is convenient for salads, soups, and side dishes because it is already cooked.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Corn provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamin, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids such as lutein and zeaxanthin help protect eye health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands add salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Bisphenol A in cans
items.content: Long‑term storage in metal cans can lead to BPA migration; choose BPA‑free products when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, omelets, or used as a filling for tortillas. It can also be quickly warmed in a skillet with herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, transfer the corn to an airtight container and keep it refrigerated for up to 3‑4 days.

green-beans-canned-cooked-with-oil.title: Green beans, canned, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green beans cooked in vegetable oil are selected bean pods harvested at peak maturity, blanched, and sealed in airtight jars with added oil to preserve flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans retain notable amounts of B‑group vitamins and vitamin C even after being canned in oil.
Canning in oil helps the beans keep a firmer bite compared with beans packed in brine.
These cans are a staple in Mediterranean cuisines, where they are used in salads, stews, and as side dishes.
The oil acts as a natural preservative, reducing the need for synthetic additives.
Green beans in oil are often served alongside meat dishes and incorporated into pastas and risottos.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Protein contributes to tissue repair and helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The beans provide vitamins A, C, K, as well as iron and potassium, important for immunity and blood‑pressure regulation.

items.title: Beneficial fats from oil
items.content: The added vegetable oil supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Canned green beans contain virtually no sugar, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned products can be high in salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Caloric density from oil
items.content: The oil adds extra calories, which should be considered in weight‑management plans.

items.title: Bisphenol A in packaging
items.content: If the can has an epoxy liner, there is a minimal risk of BPA migration; choose brands with BPA‑free packaging when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Green beans in oil can be eaten straight from the jar, tossed into salads, mixed into pasta, added to omelets, or served as a side to meat and fish. For a lighter option, drain the oil and briefly warm the beans in a skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the beans in the original container in the refrigerator and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Imitation crab meat (often called crab sticks) is a processed seafood product made primarily from white fish such as pollock, combined with flavorings, colorants, and crab‑like seasoning. It has a mild, slightly sweet taste and a firm, fibrous texture that mimics real crab meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial crab‑like product was created in Japan in the 1970s and called “kani kamaboko”.
The characteristic crab flavor is achieved with a blend of sea salt, sugar, natural crab extracts and artificial flavorings.
The pink hue comes from food‑grade colorants such as carmine or annatto.
It is a staple in sushi, salads and snack dishes because of its low cost and long shelf life.
Imitation crab contains less cholesterol than real crab but can be high in sodium.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with real crab, imitation versions usually have less total fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Provides a moderate amount of animal‑derived protein that supports muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12 and B6, which are important for red blood cell formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Provides iodine, selenium and zinc, nutrients important for thyroid function and immunity.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: A 100 g serving typically supplies about 95 kcal, making it a convenient option for calorie‑controlled meals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: To enhance flavor, the product often contains a lot of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Fish and shellfish allergy
items.content: Since it is made from fish, it can trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to seafood.

items.title: Additives and colorants
items.content: Artificial flavorings and food colorings may not be suitable for everyone.

items.title: Contains MSG
items.content: Some varieties include monosodium glutamate, which can cause headaches in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Imitation crab is used in sushi rolls, salads, pasta dishes, soups and appetizers. Before use, it is usually sliced into strips or cubes. A quick sauté in a little oil can enhance its flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and consume within 3–5 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, though the texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pizza is a popular fast‑food dish consisting of a dough base topped with tomato sauce and a generous layer of melted cheese. It is commonly served in fast‑food chains and pizzerias.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese layer can include mozzarella, cheddar, parmesan, or a blend of these.
The classic Italian Margherita pizza is considered the ancestor of the modern cheese pizza.
In the United States, cheese pizza ranks among the top‑5 best‑selling items in fast‑food menus.
Thick‑crust dough usually contains more yeast and a longer proofing time, making it puffier.
There is a “four‑cheese” variant that uses four different cheeses for a richer flavor.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese is rich in calcium, which supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The cheese topping provides a substantial amount of animal protein, aiding tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese contains vitamins B2 and B12, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Certain cheeses (e.g., mozzarella) contain live cultures that can benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat in cheese helps promote a feeling of fullness.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Cheese pizza can be calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consumption.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese often contains a lot of salt, which can be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to casein.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese pizza is typically eaten hot, sliced into wedges. Additional toppings such as fresh vegetables, olives, or herbs can be added to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover pizza in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to keep the crust crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled turnip is the root vegetable turnip (Brassica rapa subsp. rapa) that has been cured in a brine of vinegar, spices, and sometimes sugar. The process gives it a bright pink or orange hue, a crisp texture, and a mildly sweet‑sour flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled turnip is a classic accompaniment to vodka in Russian cuisine.
Traditional recipes use vinegar, sugar, salt, mustard seeds and coriander.
Turnips are rich in vitamin C, though some of it is lost during pickling.
In some countries it is served as a “turnip salad” with carrots and onions.
The vivid color can be achieved with food coloring or beet juice.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Pickled turnip provides few calories, making it suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in turnip help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium in turnip contributes to normal blood pressure.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The brine’s salt can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Vinegar acidity
items.content: Vinegar may irritate the stomach in individuals with acid reflux.

items.title: Mustard seed allergy
items.content: Some recipes include mustard seeds, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Bacterial risk if improperly stored
items.content: Leaving pickled turnip at room temperature too long can allow bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled turnip is enjoyed as a snack, in sandwiches, salads, or as part of a cold‑cut platter. It adds a bright flavor to cabbage, potato or carrot salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pickled turnip in the refrigerator in a sealed jar. When kept properly, it retains flavor and crunch for 2–3 months. Discard if mold appears or an off‑odor develops.
